- **The header has a `kid`.** Only keys with that `kid` are candidates. Among them, exactly one must have the header's `alg`: none is `alg_mismatch`, and several is `ambiguous_key`. When no key has that `kid`, a key with no `kid` at all stands in: exactly one such key must have the header's `alg`, several is `ambiguous_key`, and none is `unknown_kid`. That is how a single PEM key, which has no `kid`, verifies tokens from an issuer that names its key in every token. A remote set refetches its JWKS before letting a key without a `kid` stand in, as it does for an unknown `kid`, so a key rotated in under a new `kid` is found.
- **The header has no `kid`.** Exactly one key in the whole set must have the header's `alg`. None is `no_matching_key`, and several is `ambiguous_key`.

So a set may hold one key per algorithm without `kid`s, but once it holds two keys of one algorithm, tokens must name their key. A secret key only ever matches tokens of its own HMAC algorithm and a public key only its own algorithm, since both follow from the `alg` comparison.

## A local key set

```ts
import { createKeySet, createVerifier, type PublicKey } from "@codenhub/jwt";

declare const currentKey: PublicKey; // kid "2026-10"
declare const previousKey: PublicKey; // kid "2026-07"

const verify = createVerifier({
  keys: createKeySet([currentKey, previousKey]),
  issuer: "https://issuer.example",
});
```

`createKeySet` takes public and secret keys this package created, and copies the list, so changing your array later does not change the set. It throws a `TypeError` for an empty list, a private key, an object this package did not create, or two keys with the same `kid` and `alg`, including two keys without a `kid` and with the same `alg`, which selection could never tell apart.

The set lists its keys in `keys`, a frozen array in the order you gave them. An issuer that verifies its own tokens with the set can publish its JWKS from the same list, so the two never disagree:

```ts
import { createKeySet, exportPublicJwk, type PublicKey } from "@codenhub/jwt";

const keys = createKeySet([currentKey, previousKey]);

const jwks = {
  keys: await Promise.all(keys.keys.filter((key): key is PublicKey => key.kind === "public").map(async (key) => exportPublicJwk(key))),
};
// Serve JSON.stringify(jwks) at your jwks_uri.
```

The filter keeps secret keys out of the document, where `exportPublicJwk` would refuse them anyway. To also choose the key that signs, and when each key is published, use a key ring instead: [Key rotation](docs/rotation.md).

## Importing a JWKS

A JWKS (JSON Web Key Set) is a JSON object whose `keys` member is an array of JWKs. `importKeySet` imports the public keys of one:

```ts
import { importKeySet } from "@codenhub/jwt";

const result = await importKeySet(JSON.parse(jwksText), { algorithms: ["RS256"] });
if (result.ok) {
  const keys = result.value;
}
```

A JWKS is untrusted input, so the import never throws for it. It fails only when the document is not a JWKS at all: `malformed` when it is not an object or its `keys` is not an array (path `["keys"]`), and `too_large` with `{ limit: "keys", maximum: 100 }` when it lists more than 100 keys.

Individual keys that cannot be used are skipped, not fatal, because an issuer's JWKS routinely holds keys meant for something else, such as encryption. Skipped are: `oct` keys (a JWKS is public, so a secret never comes from one), keys with `use` other than `sig`, keys with private members, weak, oversized or malformed keys, and keys whose `alg` is not in `algorithms`. A JWKS with no usable key gives an empty set, whose `select` always fails. To read a recipient's encryption keys instead, use `importEncryptionKeySet` or `createRemoteEncryptionKeySet`; [Encrypting tokens](docs/encrypting.md#a-recipients-encryption-keys) explains.

Each usable key becomes one key per algorithm it is bound to:

- A JWK with an `alg` member is bound to that algorithm, if `algorithms` allows it.
- A JWK without `alg` is bound to every allowed algorithm its `kty` and `crv` fit. An `RSA` key becomes one key for each of `RS256`, `RS384`, `RS512`, `PS256`, `PS384` and `PS512`; an `EC` key one for the algorithm of its curve; an `OKP` `Ed25519` key an `EdDSA` key and an `Ed25519` key. The token's `alg` then picks between them, which is safe because both are the same family of signature on the same key.

`algorithms` defaults to every asymmetric algorithm, a list that may grow in a minor release. Narrow it to what your issuer actually uses, so a key the issuer meant only for `RS256` is never used to check a `PS256` token.

Two usable keys with the same `kid` and `alg` do not fail the import; selecting them fails with `ambiguous_key` rather than picking one.

The imported set's `keys` lists one key per JWK and algorithm it was bound to, in the JWKS's order, so an RSA JWK without `alg` appears six times.

## Keys of several issuers

A verifier's `issuer` option says which issuers it accepts, but not which issuer each key speaks for. When one verifier holds the keys of several issuers, such as one per tenant, any of those keys would verify a token claiming any accepted `iss`: tenant A's key, or anyone who holds it, could sign a token that says it comes from tenant B. Give each issuer's key set the `issuer` option, which `createKeySet`, `importKeySet` and `createRemoteKeySet` all take:

```ts
const tenantA = createRemoteKeySet({ url: "https://a.issuer.example/jwks.json", issuer: "https://a.issuer.example" });
```

Each key the set hands out is then bound to that issuer, and its `issuer` member says so. A verifier that selects a bound key requires the token's `iss` to equal it, whatever its own `issuer` option allows: a missing `iss` is `missing_claim` with `{ claim: "iss" }`, and a different one is `wrong_issuer`. The binding travels with the key, so it holds in a key set built from other key sets, as in [your own key set](#your-own-key-set).

`createKeySet` binds copies of the keys you give it and leaves the originals unbound; a copy works wherever the original does. A key already bound to the same issuer is kept as it is, and one bound to another issuer throws a `TypeError`, since a key cannot speak for two issuers.

### Choosing the key set by issuer

To reach those sets from one verifier, give `createVerifier` a function as `keys`. It is called with the issuer the token claims and the token's header, and returns that issuer's key set, or `undefined` for an issuer it does not know:

```ts
import { createRemoteKeySet, createVerifier, type KeySet } from "@codenhub/jwt";

const tenants = new Map<string, KeySet>(["https://a.issuer.example", "https://b.issuer.example"].map((issuer) => [issuer, createRemoteKeySet({ url: `${issuer}/jwks.json`, issuer })]));

const verify = createVerifier({ keys: (issuer) => tenants.get(issuer), audience: "https://api.example" });
```

The verifier reads `iss` from the payload before the signature is checked, only to route the token: a token without `iss` is `missing_claim` with `{ claim: "iss" }`, one whose `iss` is not a string is `invalid_claim`, and an `iss` the function returns `undefined` for is `wrong_issuer`. When the verifier also has an `issuer` option, an `iss` it does not list is `wrong_issuer` before the function is called. The function may be `async`. If it throws, rejects, or returns something other than a key set or a route, the token fails with `key_fetch_failed` and `{ reason: "key_set_error" }`, and `onKeySetError` gets the error.

When issuers' tokens name different audiences or `typ` values, as tenants with their own client IDs do, return a route instead of the key set: `{ keys, audience, type }`. A route's `audience` and `type` take the same values as the verifier options and replace them for that issuer's tokens; one it leaves out keeps the verifier's. A route that is invalid, including one with any member besides `keys`, `audience` and `type`, such as a misspelled `audiences`, is `key_set_error`, like any other mistake in the function.

```ts
const verify = createVerifier({
  keys: (issuer) => {
    const tenant = tenantsByIssuer.get(issuer);
    return tenant && { keys: tenant.keySet, audience: tenant.clientId };
  },
});
```

The `iss` is chosen by whoever sent the token. Look it up among issuers you already hold, as the `Map` above does, and never build a JWKS URL or a database query from it without checking it against a list first: otherwise anyone can make your server fetch from an address they pick. Still give each set its `issuer`: the function picks the set by a claim the signature has not yet covered, and the binding is what then refuses a token whose key belongs to another issuer.

## A remote key set

`createRemoteKeySet` fetches an issuer's JWKS from a URL, imports it as `importKeySet` does, and caches it:

```ts
import { createRemoteKeySet, createVerifier } from "@codenhub/jwt";

const keys = createRemoteKeySet({
  url: "https://issuer.example/.well-known/jwks.json",
  algorithms: ["RS256"],
});

const verify = createVerifier({ keys, issuer: "https://issuer.example", audience: "api" });
```

Nothing is fetched until the first token needs a key. Create the key set once and share it between requests, so they share its cache.

The URL is fetched as given. The package refuses plain `http:` except on a loopback host, but it cannot tell whether a name or address is internal to your network. When the URL comes from someone else, such as the `jwks_uri` a client registered with your OpenID Provider for `private_key_jwt` or encrypted tokens, check it before creating the set: require `https:`, and refuse hosts that resolve to loopback, private or link-local addresses, or allow only hosts you know. Otherwise a client chooses where your server sends requests, and learns from the failures whether something answered there.

On Cloudflare Workers, also pass `waitUntil` from `cloudflare:workers`. A Worker cancels a request's unfinished I/O once the request has responded, and that includes a JWKS fetch the key set started in the background. With `waitUntil`, each fetch keeps running until it is done:

```ts
import { waitUntil } from "cloudflare:workers";

const keys = createRemoteKeySet({ url: "https://issuer.example/.well-known/jwks.json", waitUntil });
```

Without it, nothing breaks. The cache is just replaced later: background fetches die with their requests, so the expired JWKS keeps being used until `maxStale` runs out and a token waits for a fetch of its own.

### Options

Durations are in seconds. Every option is checked when the key set is created, and an invalid one throws a `TypeError`, as does a name that is not an option below (`createRemoteKeySet: options.cachettl is not an option.`).

| Option             | Default                        | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `url`              | required                       | An absolute `https:` URL, as a string or a `URL`, or `http:` on `localhost`, `127.0.0.0/8` or `[::1]` for local development. Anything else, and URLs with a user name or password, throw.                          |
| `fetch`            | `globalThis.fetch`             | A `JwksFetch`, `(url: string, init: RequestInit) => Promise<Response>`, for runtimes or tests that supply their own. The global is looked up at each fetch.                                                        |
| `algorithms`       | every asymmetric algorithm     | As for [`importKeySet`](#importing-a-jwks).                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `issuer`           | none                           | The issuer whose JWKS this is. Each key is bound to it, so a token it verifies must carry that `iss`. See [keys of several issuers](#keys-of-several-issuers).                                                     |
| `cacheTtl`         | `600`                          | Most time a fetched JWKS is used before it is fetched again; a shorter `max-age` shortens it, to `cooldown` at least. An integer of at least 1.                                                                    |
| `cooldown`         | `30`, or `cacheTtl` if smaller | Least time between the starts of two fetches caused by a failure or an unknown `kid`. An integer from 0 through `cacheTtl`.                                                                                        |
| `maxStale`         | `3600`                         | How long after `cacheTtl` ran out the last JWKS is still used while a new one is fetched, or while fetching it fails. An integer of at least 0; 0 never uses an expired JWKS.                                      |
| `timeout`          | `5`                            | How long one fetch, body included, may take. Greater than 0 and at most 60; fractions are allowed.                                                                                                                 |
| `maxResponseBytes` | `65536`                        | Largest response body accepted, in bytes. An integer from 1 through 1048576.                                                                                                                                       |
| `now`              | `Date.now`                     | The current time in milliseconds, for tests.                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `seed`             | none                           | `{ url, jwks, fetchedAt }` as `onFetch` got it, used as if this key set had fetched it. `null` is none; one of another shape or `url`, or with no usable key, is ignored. See [persisting](#persisting-the-cache). |
| `onFetch`          | none                           | Called with `{ url, jwks, fetchedAt }` after each successful fetch.                                                                                                                                                |
| `onFetchError`     | none                           | Called with the `key_fetch_failed` issue after each failed fetch, including fetches no token waited for and fetches a newer one replaced.                                                                          |
| `waitUntil`        | none                           | Called with each fetch as it starts, to keep it running after the request that started it has responded. On Cloudflare Workers, pass `waitUntil` from `cloudflare:workers`.                                        |

### Caching and rotation

- **Expiry.** A fetched JWKS is used for `cacheTtl` seconds, counted from when the fetch finished. When the response's `Cache-Control` has a shorter `max-age`, it is used for that long instead, but never for less than `cooldown`, which is also what `no-store` and `no-cache` give it; `s-maxage` and a malformed `max-age` are ignored. So an issuer that announces a short lifetime before a rotation is fetched again sooner, and `cacheTtl` stays the upper bound. The first token after that is still verified with it, at once, and starts a fetch in the background that replaces it for later tokens. Past `maxStale`, tokens wait for the fetch instead.
- **One fetch at a time.** While a fetch is running, a token waits for it only when the cached JWKS cannot give its key; concurrent requests never start a second fetch. A token waits at most until a second past the fetch's `timeout`. If the fetch has not finished by then, or fails because the request that started it has ended, the token's request fetches again itself, unless the cooldown is running and the cached JWKS is still usable: then it selects from the cache. A fetch that has not settled a second past its `timeout`, and past the cooldown, no longer counts as running. Both happen on Cloudflare Workers when the request that started the fetch ended and took its I/O with it, unless `waitUntil` kept it alive.
- **Unknown `kid`.** When an issuer rotates in a new key, the first token signed with it names a `kid` your cached JWKS does not hold. The key set then fetches the JWKS once more and selects again from the result, also when a key without a `kid` could stand in for it; if that refetch fails, the stand-in still answers. A header without a `kid` never causes a refetch.
- **Cooldown.** A refetch for an unknown `kid`, and a retry after a failed fetch, only starts once `cooldown` seconds have passed since the last fetch started. Inside that window an unknown `kid` fails with `unknown_kid` at once. Anyone can send you tokens with invented `kid`s; with the cooldown, a flood of them costs the issuer at most one request per window, however many tokens arrive.
- **Stale keys.** When a fetch fails after `cacheTtl` ran out, the last JWKS that was fetched is still used for up to `maxStale` more seconds, so a short outage at the issuer does not take your service down with it. Using it does not extend it: each token after the cooldown tries to fetch again, and past `maxStale` the key set fails with `key_fetch_failed`. Lower `maxStale` if a revoked key must stop working sooner, at the cost of failing sooner when the issuer is unreachable.

### Persisting the cache

A process that lives for one request, such as a serverless function, starts with an empty cache and fetches the JWKS on its first token. To skip that, save what `onFetch` receives and pass it back as `seed`:

```ts
const saved = await store.get("jwks"); // the string stored last time, or null when there is none

const keys = createRemoteKeySet({
  url: "https://issuer.example/.well-known/jwks.json",
  seed: saved ? JSON.parse(saved) : null,
  onFetch: (snapshot) => store.put("jwks", JSON.stringify(snapshot)),
});
```

A seed is treated exactly like a JWKS this key set fetched at `fetchedAt`: fresh for `cacheTtl`, then stale for `maxStale`, then not used at all. `null` and `undefined` mean no seed. A seed that is not a snapshot, such as one an older build saved without `url`, is ignored, and so is one whose `jwks` imports no key this set can use: the key set fetches as it would without one. A seed whose `url` is not this key set's, compared as the URL parser normalizes both, is ignored too, so a staging key set's snapshot saved under the same store key never gets its keys bound to the production `issuer`. Give each key set its own store key anyway, or they keep overwriting each other's snapshot. `onFetch` and `onFetchError` may return a promise, which is handed to `waitUntil` so a save outlives the request on Workers; what they throw or reject with is ignored, so a broken store or logger never fails a token.

A seed or cache whose `fetchedAt` is up to a minute ahead of the clock, as after a small clock correction or from a host whose clock runs ahead, counts as just fetched. Further ahead, it is expired: a clock that jumps back that far could otherwise keep a removed key trusted past `cacheTtl` plus `maxStale`. A clock that steps back while a fetch is running makes that fetch count as just started, so it is neither replaced by a second one nor held running for as long as the step; a cooldown that is not covering a running fetch ends when the clock steps back before its start.

### When fetching fails

A fetch is a `GET` with `accept: application/json` and `cache: "no-cache"`, so a browser's HTTP cache revalidates the JWKS with the issuer rather than answering a refetch from its copy. A runtime that rejects the `cache` member, as Cloudflare Workers does before compatibility date 2025-08-07, is asked again without it, and the key set leaves it out from then on. A fetch does not follow redirects and accepts only status 200. The body is read up to `maxResponseBytes` and abandoned as soon as it grows past that, and the whole fetch, body included, is abandoned after `timeout`. The body must be a strict JSON object, parsed with the same rules as a token's header, after one leading UTF-8 byte order mark, which some servers write, is dropped; then a JWKS with at least one key the set can use. The response's `Content-Type` is not checked: only the configured URL is ever fetched, and the body has to parse as a JWKS whatever it is labelled. A failed fetch never replaces the keys the set already has.

A failure the stale keys cannot cover is `key_fetch_failed`, whose `params.reason` says what happened:

| `reason`           | Cause                                                                                            |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `timeout`          | The fetch took longer than `timeout`.                                                            |
| `network`          | `fetch` rejected, for example because the host could not be reached.                             |
| `status`           | The response status was not 200, redirects included. `params.status` holds the status code.      |
| `too_large`        | The `Content-Length` header or the body exceeded `maxResponseBytes`.                             |
| `invalid_response` | The body was not a strict JSON object, was not a JWKS, or listed more than 100 keys.             |
| `no_usable_keys`   | The JWKS held no key this set can use: none at all, none for `algorithms`, or none that imports. |

The issue holds nothing from the response. `select` never throws and never rejects, whatever the server sends. The one exception is a bug in your own `now` option: when it returns something other than a finite number, `select` rejects with a `TypeError`, because a `NaN` clock would keep the cache from ever expiring. A verifier that calls such a key set turns the rejection into `key_fetch_failed` with `{ reason: "key_set_error" }`, so it fails closed.

## Your own key set

`KeySet` is an interface with one method, `select(header)`, which returns a promise of a result holding a key. You can implement it, for example to choose an issuer's key set by a prefix in the `kid`, when the tokens name their tenant that way rather than by `iss` as [choosing the key set by issuer](#choosing-the-key-set-by-issuer) does:

```ts
import { createRemoteKeySet, type KeySet } from "@codenhub/jwt";

const tenants = new Map<string, KeySet>([
  ["a", createRemoteKeySet({ url: "https://a.issuer.example/jwks.json", issuer: "https://a.issuer.example" })],
  ["b", createRemoteKeySet({ url: "https://b.issuer.example/jwks.json", issuer: "https://b.issuer.example" })],
]);

const keys: KeySet = {
  select: async (header) => {
    const tenant = tenants.get(header.kid?.split(":")[0] ?? "");
    return tenant === undefined ? { ok: false, error: { issues: [{ code: "unknown_kid", path: ["header", "kid"] }] } } : tenant.select(header);
  },
};
```

Each tenant's set has its `issuer`, so tenant A's key verifies only tokens whose `iss` is tenant A's, whichever `kid` the token names. Without it, a token signed with tenant A's key and claiming tenant B's `iss` would pass, as the `kid` alone picks the key. A verifier's `issuer` option still says which issuers it accepts at all.

A verifier treats a custom key set as code that may be wrong. If `select` throws, rejects, or returns anything other than a result holding a public or secret key this package created, the verifier fails with `key_fetch_failed` and `{ reason: "key_set_error" }` instead of throwing or using what it returned. A failed result is passed through when each of its issues has a string `code`, and a `path` that is absent or an array of strings and finite numbers, such as `{ code: "tenant_unknown", path: ["tenant"] }`; any other failure is `key_set_error` too. Each issue is copied with its `code`, `path` and `params`, so keep them free of token values as this package's own are.

The issue never carries the error, which may hold anything. To log it, pass `onKeySetError` to `createVerifier`: it is called with what `select` or the `keys` function threw or rejected with, or with a `TypeError` naming what it returned instead. It is not called for a failure the key set returns itself, such as `unknown_kid`, and its own errors are ignored.

```ts
const verify = createVerifier({ keys: tenantKeys, onKeySetError: (error) => logger.error("key set failed", error) });
```

Keys are recognized only by the copy of `@codenhub/jwt` that created them. If your program loads two copies, `createKeySet` throws the `TypeError` meant for look-alikes ("… not a look-alike object") for a key from the other copy, and when a verifier's key set, one from the other copy or a custom one, selects such a key, the token fails with `key_fetch_failed` and `{ reason: "key_set_error" }`. Deduplicate the install so one copy is loaded, and if you publish a library built on this package, declare it as a `peerDependency`. [Keys](docs/keys.md) explains why.

<!-- Source: docs/rotation.md -->

# Key rotation

An issuer that rotates its signing key has to get the order right. A verifier caches your JWKS, so a key must be published before the first token it signs reaches one, or that token fails with `unknown_kid` until the cache expires. And a key must stay published after it stops signing, until every token it signed has expired. `createKeyRing` keeps that schedule for you: you give it your keys and when each one starts signing, and it tells you which key signs now and which keys to publish.

## A key ring

```ts
import { createKeyRing, createVerifier, sign, type PrivateKey } from "@codenhub/jwt";

declare const currentKey: PrivateKey; // kid "2026-11"
declare const nextKey: PrivateKey; // kid "2026-12"

const ring = createKeyRing({
  keys: [
    { key: currentKey, activeFrom: 1_793_491_200 }, // 2026-11-01T00:00:00Z
    { key: nextKey, activeFrom: 1_796_083_200 }, // 2026-12-01T00:00:00Z
  ],
  publishAhead: 86_400, // one day
  publishAfter: 7_200, // two hours: the longest token lifetime plus clock tolerance
});

const token = await sign({
  payload: { iss: "https://issuer.example", sub: "user-1" },
  key: ring.signingKey(),
  issuedAt: true,
  expiresIn: 3600,
});

const verify = createVerifier({ keys: ring, issuer: "https://issuer.example" });

// At your jwks_uri:
const body = JSON.stringify(await ring.jwks());
```

- **`activeFrom`** is when a key starts signing, in seconds since the Unix epoch, like `exp`. A key signs until the next key's `activeFrom`. **`retiredAt`**, optional, stops it earlier, when it must leave service with no successor yet.
- **`signingKey()`** returns the key whose `activeFrom` came last, unless it is retired. It never falls back to a key a later one replaced. When no key signs, because every `activeFrom` is still to come or the newest active key is retired, it throws a `TypeError`: signing with no key is a configuration mistake, not something a request can recover from.
- **`jwks()`** resolves to the frozen JWKS of every key published now: from `publishAhead` seconds before its `activeFrom` until `publishAfter` seconds after it stops signing. It holds public keys only, also for keys that are not extractable or live in a KMS.
- **The ring is a key set.** Its `select` chooses from the same keys `jwks()` publishes, so your own services accept exactly the keys other verifiers can see. Pass `issuer` to bind them, as [key sets](docs/key-sets.md#keys-of-several-issuers) explains.

Every key needs a `kid`, unique in the ring, since tokens must name the key that signed them once two are published; `generateKeyPair({ kid: "thumbprint" })` gives one. Two keys may not share an `activeFrom`, and a ring holds at most 100 keys, the most a JWKS may list for this package's key sets. Keys may use different algorithms, but verifiers that accept only some algorithms must accept the new one before its `activeFrom`. A ring checks every option when it is created and throws a `TypeError` for an invalid one, as for a name that is not an option.

The ring stores nothing and reads the clock, `now`, at every call. Keep your keys and their times in your own storage, and build the ring from them at startup, or per request on a serverless platform. Every instance built from the same records signs with the same key at the same second, give or take their clocks; around a switch both keys are published, so an instance whose clock runs ahead is harmless.

## Choosing the durations

**`publishAhead`** must cover every copy of your JWKS a verifier may hold: the `max-age` you serve it with, plus any shared cache in between, plus how long a verifier keeps using a JWKS it cannot refresh. For this package's remote key sets that last part is `maxStale`, one hour by default. A day is a comfortable value for scheduled rotation.

**`publishAfter`** must outlast every token the key signed: your longest token lifetime plus the clock tolerance of your verifiers. A key that leaves the JWKS sooner makes its last tokens fail with `unknown_kid` before they expire.

Serve the JWKS with a `max-age` well below `publishAhead`:

```ts
return new Response(JSON.stringify(await ring.jwks()), {
  headers: { "content-type": "application/json", "cache-control": "public, max-age=3600" },
});
```

A remote key set never caches longer than the `max-age` it is sent, or its `cooldown` when that is longer, so this also bounds how long a key you removed stays trusted elsewhere: `max-age` plus the verifier's `maxStale`. A set started from a [`seed`](docs/key-sets.md#persisting-the-cache) is the exception: a snapshot does not record `max-age`, so the seeded keys are kept for the verifier's `cacheTtl`, and a removed key stays trusted for up to `cacheTtl` plus `maxStale` there. Count on the longer bound when verifiers you do not run may seed their sets.

## Rotating

1. **Add the next key** with an `activeFrom` at least `publishAhead` seconds from now. Generate it, store it with its `activeFrom`, and rebuild the ring. It appears in the JWKS at once, or when its publication starts.
2. **Wait.** At its `activeFrom`, `signingKey()` returns the new key; nothing else changes. The old key stays in the JWKS for `publishAfter` seconds more.
3. **Delete the old key** from your storage once it is out of the JWKS, at the new key's `activeFrom` plus `publishAfter`. A ring ignores keys past their publication, so deleting late is harmless; deleting early ends their tokens early.

An `activeFrom` already in the past is accepted, since the ring cannot know when you first published the key. A key added that way signs at once, and verifiers that cached your JWKS before it was added do not have it: this package's remote key sets fetch again for an unknown `kid`, at most once per `cooldown`, but others may fail until their cache expires.

## Encryption keys

A recipient that publishes keys for senders to encrypt to, such as an OpenID client whose ID tokens are encrypted, rotates them with `createEncryptionKeyRing`. It takes JWE private keys from `generateJweKeyPair` or `importJwePrivateKey`, with `activeFrom` and `retiredAt` as above. It has no `issuer`, which concerns who signs, and no `publishAhead`, since it publishes only the current key. Signing and encryption keys rotate in separate rings, and each refuses the other kind with a `TypeError` naming the right function, so a signing ring's bundle carries no JWE code.

```ts
import { createDecrypter, createEncryptionKeyRing, type JwePrivateKey } from "@codenhub/jwt";

declare const currentKey: JwePrivateKey; // kid "enc-2026-11"
declare const nextKey: JwePrivateKey; // kid "enc-2026-12"

const ring = createEncryptionKeyRing({
  keys: [
    { key: currentKey, activeFrom: 1_793_491_200 },
    { key: nextKey, activeFrom: 1_796_083_200 },
  ],
  publishAfter: 172_800, // senders' JWKS cache, plus how long a token takes to reach you
});

const decrypt = createDecrypter({ keys: ring });
const body = JSON.stringify(await ring.jwks());
```

- **`encryptionKey()`** returns the public half of the newest active key, the key to encrypt to now, such as for tokens you encrypt to yourself. It throws when no key is active, as `signingKey()` does.
- **`jwks()`** publishes that key alone, with `use: "enc"`, and no key when none is active. A sender that picks a key by algorithm, as `createRemoteEncryptionKeySet`'s `select({ alg })` does, never finds two, even while a switch is under way.
- **The ring is the decryption key set.** Its `select` chooses the private key from every key that decrypts now: from its `activeFrom` until `publishAfter` seconds after the next key's `activeFrom` or its own `retiredAt`. A sender that read your JWKS before a switch keeps encrypting to the old key until its copy expires, and its tokens may arrive later still. A key whose `activeFrom` is still to come decrypts nothing, since no sender has been given it.

Choose `publishAfter` to cover the old key's last tokens: your JWKS `max-age`, plus how long senders keep a JWKS they cannot refresh (`maxStale` for this package's remote key sets), plus how long a token may take to reach you. A switch needs no lead time: senders that still hold the old key encrypt to it, and it still decrypts.

## Replacing a leaked key

A leaked key must stop signing and stop verifying now, not after `publishAfter`. Delete it from your storage and add a new key with `activeFrom` of the current time. Tokens the leaked key signed stop verifying with your ring at once, and with other verifiers when their copy of your JWKS expires. The new key is not in those copies, so expect `unknown_kid` failures for up to your `max-age` from verifiers that do not refetch for an unknown `kid`; that is the price of the emergency path.

<!-- Source: docs/dpop.md -->

# DPoP proofs

DPoP (RFC 9449) binds an access token to a key the client holds. With each request, the client sends a proof: a short-lived JWT signed with its private key, carrying the public key in a `jwk` header and naming the request it is for. A server accepts the request only when the proof verifies and its key is the one the access token is bound to, so a stolen access token is useless without the key.

`createDpopProof` signs proofs on the client, and `createDpopVerifier` checks them on the server.

## Creating proofs

Generate the client's key once and sign a new proof for every request:

```ts
import { createDpopProof, generateKeyPair } from "@codenhub/jwt";

const { privateKey } = await generateKeyPair({ alg: "ES256" });

// At the token endpoint: no access token yet.
const tokenProof = await createDpopProof({ key: privateKey, method: "POST", url: "https://issuer.example/token" });

// At a resource server: the proof carries the hash of the access token it comes with.
const proof = await createDpopProof({ key: privateKey, method: "GET", url: "https://api.example/orders", accessToken });
await fetch("https://api.example/orders", { headers: { authorization: `DPoP ${accessToken}`, dpop: proof } });
```

The proof's header is `alg`, from the key, `typ: "dpop+jwt"`, and `jwk`, the key's public half with only its material. The key's own `kid` is not written, since the `jwk` names the key. The payload is:

| Claim   | Value                                                                                                                                |
| ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `jti`   | `jti`, or a random UUID by default.                                                                                                  |
| `htm`   | `method`, as given. Methods are case-sensitive, so send `GET`, not `get`.                                                            |
| `htu`   | `url`, a string or a `URL`, normalized and without its query and fragment: `https://API.example:443/a?x` is `https://api.example/a`. |
| `iat`   | The clock, `now` or `Date.now`, in whole seconds.                                                                                    |
| `ath`   | When `accessToken` is given, the base64url SHA-256 hash of it.                                                                       |
| `nonce` | When `nonce` is given: the value the server last sent in a `DPoP-Nonce` header.                                                      |

The key must be a private key of an asymmetric algorithm. A non-extractable key, kept in IndexedDB as [Keys](docs/keys.md#importing-a-web-crypto-key) shows, and a key held by a KMS through `createExternalSigningKey` both work. A secret key throws: a proof anyone holding the secret could sign proves nothing.

## Verifying proofs

Create the verifier once, at startup, and call it with each request's `DPoP` header:

```ts
import { createDpopVerifier } from "@codenhub/jwt";

const verifyProof = createDpopVerifier({ algorithms: ["ES256", "EdDSA"] });

const result = await verifyProof(request.headers.get("dpop"), { method: request.method, url: request.url });
if (!result.ok) {
  return new Response(null, { status: 400, headers: { "www-authenticate": 'DPoP error="invalid_dpop_proof"' } });
}
const { payload, key, thumbprint } = result.value;
```

`thumbprint` is the RFC 7638 thumbprint of the proof's key. At the token endpoint, write it into the access token you issue as `cnf: { jkt: thumbprint }`; that binds the token to the key.

A proof goes through these checks in order, and the first failure among the first six is the result:

1. The length cap, `maxLength`, then the same strict parsing as any token's.
2. `typ` is exactly `dpop+jwt`, or `wrong_type`.
3. `alg` is one of `algorithms`, every asymmetric algorithm by default, or `unsupported_alg`. A symmetric algorithm is never accepted.
4. The `jwk` header is an object, or `malformed` at `["header", "jwk"]`.
5. It is a public JWK for that `alg`, imported with every check `importPublicKey` runs. A failure keeps its code with the path under `["header", "jwk"]`, such as `unexpected_private_key` at `["header", "jwk", "d"]` for a JWK with a private member.
6. The signature verifies with that key, or `bad_signature`.

Then the claims, with every failure reported together:

- `jti`, `htm`, `htu` and `iat` are present (`missing_claim`) and of their types (`invalid_claim`). `exp` is checked when present.
- `iat` is at most `maxAge` seconds old, 60 by default, plus `clockTolerance` (`too_old`), and at most `max(clockTolerance, 60)` seconds ahead (`issued_in_future`).
- `htm` equals the request's method exactly (`wrong_method`).
- `htu` equals the request's URL once both are normalized and stripped of their query and fragment (`wrong_url`). Normalizing lowercases the scheme and host, drops a default port, removes dot segments, decodes a percent-encoded unreserved character (`%7E` is `~`) and uppercases the hex digits of the rest (`%2f` is `%2F`). It decodes nothing else, so `%2F` never matches a `/`.
- When the request gives `accessToken`, `ath` is present (`missing_claim`) and is its hash (`wrong_access_token_hash`). Without one, `ath` is ignored.
- `jti` may be any string, an empty one included: RFC 9449 leaves its entropy to the client, and `acceptJti` sees it either way.
- A static `nonce` option, and `accessTokenClaims`, below.

Last, only for a proof that passed everything else: a `nonce` function, then `acceptJti`.

A request URL behind a proxy is the URL the client used, not the one your server sees: rebuild it from your public origin when they differ.

### Binding the access token

At a resource server, pass the access token as `accessToken` and its verified claims as `accessTokenClaims`, always both. The proof must then carry the token's hash as `ath`, and its key must have the thumbprint the token's `cnf.jkt` carries, or the proof fails with `wrong_key` at `["header", "jwk"]`:

```ts
const token = await verifyAccessToken(accessToken);
if (!token.ok) return unauthorized();

const proof = await verifyProof(request.headers.get("dpop"), {
  method: request.method,
  url: request.url,
  accessToken,
  accessTokenClaims: token.value.payload,
});
```

The verifier rejects with a `TypeError` when a request gives only one of the two. The token alone would check `ath` but never `cnf.jkt`, so a stolen token would pass with a proof signed by the thief's own key; the claims alone would leave the proof unbound to the token it came with. At the token endpoint, give neither.

Claims without a string `cnf.jkt` fail with `wrong_key` too, so a token that was never bound cannot pass as a DPoP one. A token introspection response (RFC 7662) carries `cnf.jkt` the same way and can be passed as it is.

### Nonces

A server that requires nonces (RFC 9449 §8) passes the ones it accepts as `nonce`: one value, a list, or a function that says whether a nonce is current, which may be async:

```ts
const verifyProof = createDpopVerifier({ nonce: (nonce) => nonces.isCurrent(nonce) });
```

A proof whose `nonce` is missing, not a string or not accepted fails with `wrong_nonce`, one code for all three, so the server answers it with a fresh nonce:

```ts
if (!result.ok && result.error.issues.some((issue) => issue.code === "wrong_nonce")) {
  return new Response(null, {
    status: 400, // 401 at a resource server
    headers: { "dpop-nonce": nonces.current(), "www-authenticate": 'DPoP error="use_dpop_nonce"' },
  });
}
```

Without the option, a proof's `nonce` is ignored.

### Replay

Each proof may be used once. `acceptJti` records a proof's `jti` and returns whether it was new: `false` fails the proof with `replayed`. It runs last, so a refused proof records nothing:

```ts
const verifyProof = createDpopVerifier({
  acceptJti: async (jti, { thumbprint, keepUntil }) => store.addIfAbsent(`${thumbprint}:${jti}`, keepUntil),
});
```

`keepUntil` is the last second the proof is accepted, `iat + maxAge + clockTolerance`: keep the `jti` until then, not `maxAge` after you first saw it, since a proof issued ahead of your clock is accepted that much longer. Scoping the `jti` by `thumbprint`, as above, keeps one client from blocking another's identifiers.

### Callback failures

A `nonce` function or `acceptJti` that throws, rejects or returns something other than a boolean fails the proof with `callback_failed`, with `{ option: "nonce" }` or `{ option: "acceptJti" }`. The error is kept out of the issue, which could quote anything, and goes to `onCallbackError` instead, as a key set's goes to `onKeySetError`:

```ts
const verifyProof = createDpopVerifier({ acceptJti, onCallbackError: (error) => log.error(error) });
```

Treat `callback_failed` as a server error, not the client's: answer 500 or 503.

## What throws

`createDpopProof` rejects with a `TypeError` for an input that is not one: a member that is not an option, a key that is not a private key of an asymmetric algorithm, a method that is not an HTTP method token, a URL that is not an absolute `http:` or `https:` URL, an empty `accessToken`, `nonce` or `jti`, or a clock that does not return milliseconds.

`createDpopVerifier` throws a `TypeError` for an invalid or unknown option. The verifier it returns resolves to a result for every proof, but rejects with a `TypeError` for a request that is not one, since the request comes from your code: a member that is not one of `method`, `url`, `accessToken` and `accessTokenClaims`, an invalid method or URL, an empty `accessToken`, `accessTokenClaims` that is not an object, or only one of `accessToken` and `accessTokenClaims`. [Issues](docs/errors.md) lists every code.

<!-- Source: docs/encrypting.md -->

# Encrypting tokens

A signed token proves who wrote it, and anyone holding it can read it. An encrypted token (JWE, RFC 7516) is the opposite: only the holder of the right key can read it, and on its own it proves nothing about who wrote it. `encrypt` seals bytes or text for a recipient's key, and a decrypter opens the token again:

```ts
import { createDecrypter, createJweKeySet, encrypt, generateJweKeyPair } from "@codenhub/jwt";

const recipient = await generateJweKeyPair({ alg: "ECDH-ES+A256KW", kid: "enc-2026-11" });

const token = await encrypt({ plaintext: "meet at the usual place", key: recipient.publicKey, enc: "A256GCM" });
// "eyJhbGciOiJFQ0RILUVTK0EyNTZLVyIsImVuYyI6IkEyNTZHQ00iLCJraWQiOi…" (five segments)

const decrypt = createDecrypter({ keys: createJweKeySet([recipient.privateKey]) });
const result = await decrypt(token);
if (result.ok) {
  new TextDecoder().decode(result.value.plaintext); // "meet at the usual place"
}
```

Only compact serialization is supported. As with signing, what you encrypt is your own data, so a mistake in it throws a `TypeError`; what you decrypt is someone else's, so it never throws and comes back as a result.

## Encryption keys are their own kind

JWE has its own three kinds of key, `JwePublicKey` (`kind: "jwe-public"`), `JwePrivateKey` (`"jwe-private"`) and `JweSecretKey` (`"jwe-secret"`), and they are never interchangeable with the signing keys of [Keys](docs/keys.md): `sign`, `createKeySet` and a verifier throw for an encryption key, with a message that says it is one and names the JWE functions, and `encrypt` and `createJweKeySet` throw for a signing key. Using one key both to sign and to encrypt is a cross-protocol mistake, and the types catch it before the code runs.

Each key is bound to exactly one **key management algorithm** (`alg`), the way a signing key is bound to one signature algorithm. The token's header never chooses: a decrypter fails a token whose `alg` is not its key's with `alg_mismatch`. The **content encryption algorithm** (`enc`) is chosen when encrypting, and a decrypter accepts the list in its `enc` option.

```ts
import { generateJweKeyPair, generateJweSecretKey, importJwePrivateKey, importJwePublicKey, importJweSecretKey } from "@codenhub/jwt";

const pair = await generateJweKeyPair({ alg: "RSA-OAEP-256", modulusLength: 3072, kid: "rsa-enc" });
const x25519 = await generateJweKeyPair({ alg: "ECDH-ES", crv: "X25519" });

const theirs = await importJwePublicKey(jwkFromTheirJwks, { alg: "RSA-OAEP-256" }); // result
const mine = await importJwePrivateKey(process.env.ENC_KEY_PEM, { alg: "ECDH-ES+A128KW" }); // result

const wrapping = await generateJweSecretKey({ alg: "A256KW", kid: "kek-1" });
const direct = await importJweSecretKey(thirtyTwoBytes, { alg: "dir", enc: "A256GCM" }); // result
```

The import functions take what their signing counterparts take, JWK, PEM and Web Crypto `CryptoKey`, and run the same checks for encryption: a JWK's `use`, when present, must be `enc`, its `key_ops` may hold only encryption operations, its `alg`, when present, must be the key's own, and an RSA modulus must be 2048 to 8192 bits. A key whose type or curve does not fit `alg`, as a JWK or a PEM, is `unsupported_key` at `["kty"]` or `["crv"]`: the `RSA-OAEP` algorithms take RSA, and the `ECDH-ES` algorithms take EC on P-256, P-384 or P-521, or OKP on X25519. An `EC` or `OKP` public JWK with an empty `key_ops`, which is how Web Crypto exports an ECDH or X25519 public key, is taken as stating no operations rather than as `wrong_use`. An X25519 public key of low order, one every sender would agree on an all-zero secret with, is `invalid_key`: each import runs one agreement with a fresh key to find out, as the import of a pair already does to prove its halves match. An EC key whose point is not on its curve is `invalid_key` too; the package checks the curve equation itself, because WebKit's Web Crypto imports such a point. `importJweKeyPair` returns both halves, `getJwePublicKey` the public half of a private key, `exportJwePublicJwk`, `exportJwePrivateJwk` and `exportJweSecretJwk` write JWKs with `use: "enc"`, and `exportJwePublicPem` and `exportJwePrivatePem` write SPKI and PKCS#8 PEM, without `alg` or `kid`; a secret has no PEM form. `jwkThumbprint` takes JWE keys too. A secret must be exactly as long as its algorithm's key: 16 bytes for `A128KW` and `A128GCMKW`, 32 for `A256KW` and `A256GCMKW`, and for `dir` the length of its `enc` key.

A `dir` secret is the content key itself, so it is also bound to one `enc`: `encrypt` uses it, and a decrypter fails a token naming another `enc` for it with `alg_mismatch` at `["header", "enc"]`. A JWK of a `dir` key whose `alg` names the content algorithm, as RFC 7520's cookbook writes one, is `alg_mismatch`; drop its `alg` and pass `enc` instead.

## Encrypting

`encrypt` takes the plaintext, as a `Uint8Array` or as text encrypted as its UTF-8 bytes, the key, `enc`, and an optional `header`:

```ts
const token = await encrypt({
  plaintext: new TextEncoder().encode(JSON.stringify({ balance: 1200 })),
  key: wrapping,
  enc: "A128CBC-HS256",
  header: { typ: "secret+jwe" },
});
```

`alg` comes from the key, and `enc` is required except with a `dir` key, which already names its own. A fresh content key and IV are drawn for each token, and for `ECDH-ES` a fresh ephemeral key. The whole protected header is authenticated, so changing any byte of it makes the token fail.

The IVs of AES-GCM are random 96-bit values, so a key that encrypts with AES-GCM must be replaced before it has encrypted 2^32 times, the limit NIST SP 800-38D sets on random IVs under one key. That applies to a `dir` key with `A128GCM` or `A256GCM`, whose every token is encrypted with the key itself, and to an `A128GCMKW` or `A256GCMKW` key, which wraps every token's content key with AES-GCM. The other algorithms draw a fresh content key for each token, so the limit does not build up across tokens.

`kid` defaults to the key's `kid`; `kid`, `typ` and `cty` must be strings. Other header parameters are written as given, with the JSON rules of [Signing tokens](docs/signing.md), except those that change how a token is decrypted or ask the recipient to trust a key, which throw: `crit`, `zip`, `epk`, `apu`, `apv`, `iv`, `tag`, `p2s`, `p2c`, `b64`, `jwk`, `jku`, `x5u` and `x5c`.

## Decrypting

`createDecrypter` takes:

| Option      | Default             | Meaning                                                                                                    |
| ----------- | ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `keys`      | required            | Where decryption keys come from: `createJweKeySet([...])`, or any object with a `select(header)` function. |
| `enc`       | every supported one | The content encryption algorithms accepted. Another fails with `unsupported_enc`, before any key is used.  |
| `maxLength` | 16384               | Maximum token length in characters, from 1 through 65536, checked before anything is decoded.              |

The decrypter resolves to `{ header, plaintext, key }`: the protected header, the decrypted bytes, and the key that opened the token. The header and result are frozen; `plaintext` is a fresh array that is yours. When the plaintext is JSON, `decodeJsonObject(plaintext)` reads it with the parser verifiers use, strict, depth-bounded and refusing repeated member names, and returns a result.

A decrypter's checks run in a fixed order and stop at the first failure:

1. The token is a string no longer than `maxLength`.
2. It has exactly five segments of strict base64url, and its header is a JSON object without repeated member names, with a supported `alg` and an accepted `enc`, and no `zip` or `crit`. For `A128GCMKW` and `A256GCMKW`, the header's `iv` is 96 bits and its `tag` 128 bits of strict base64url, or the token is `malformed` at `["header", "iv"]` or `["header", "tag"]`. The encrypted key is empty exactly when `alg` is `dir` or `ECDH-ES`, or the token is `malformed` at `["encrypted_key"]`, and the IV and tag have the lengths `enc` sets, or it is `malformed` at `["iv"]` or `["tag"]`; the encrypted key's own length is checked at step 5. The header is the protected one, the only header a compact token has.
3. The key set selects one key by `kid` and `alg`, as [Key sets](docs/key-sets.md#how-a-key-is-selected) describes. Keys are never tried in turn. A `dir` key is selected the same way, not by `enc`, so `createJweKeySet` refuses two `dir` keys without a `kid`, even for different `enc` values. Give them distinct `kid`s, or, when the sender writes none, as an OpenID Provider deriving keys from a `client_secret` may, use one decrypter per endpoint, each with its own key.
4. For `ECDH-ES`, the header's `epk` is imported as a public key on the private key's curve, or fails with `malformed` at `["header", "epk"]`. A P-256, P-384 or P-521 `epk` that is not on its curve fails the same way: the package checks the curve itself rather than leave it to Web Crypto, because WebKit imports such a point and agreeing on it can reveal the private key. So does an X25519 `epk` of low order, and one with the top bit of `x` set: RFC 7748 has X25519 ignore that bit, runtimes differ in whether they do, and no sender sets it, so it is refused on every runtime alike.
5. The content key is recovered, and the authentication tag is checked before any plaintext exists.

A decrypted token is not a verified one. Encrypting to a public key needs only the public key, which anyone can have, so a plaintext's claims say nothing about who wrote them until a signature does; that is what the next section is for. There is deliberately no function that reads claims from a bare JWE.

`readJweHeader(token)` reads the protected header without any key, to route a token or pick a decrypter by its `kid` or `alg` first. It checks the token as steps 1 and 2 do, with every supported `enc` accepted, takes the same `maxLength` option and default, and never decrypts. The header it returns is untrusted, since only decryption checks the tag that authenticates it.

### What a forged token learns

Steps 1 to 4 fail with codes that describe the token's shape, which the attacker already knows: a key set's `alg_mismatch` at step 3, and a bad `epk` as `malformed` at `["header", "epk"]` at step 4, stay what they are. Step 5 is where a forger probes the key, so every failure in recovering the content key or checking the tag is the same: a key that does not unwrap, an AES-GCM key wrap whose tag fails, an RSA ciphertext that does not decrypt, a wrong tag, a tampered header, IV or ciphertext all give `decryption_failed`, with no path. When unwrapping fails, a random content key stands in and the token fails on its tag (RFC 7516 §11.5), so the answer is the same either way, and the CBC tag is compared in constant time. Log `decryption_failed` freely; it never holds a byte of the token.

Refused before any cryptography, with a result rather than a throw:

- **`RSA1_5`**, which RFC 8725 warns against: its padding oracle has decrypted traffic on real servers since 1998. It is `unsupported_alg`.
- **`PBES2-*`**, password-based keys, whose iteration count the token chooses, so a hostile one costs the recipient as much work as it asks for. It is `unsupported_alg`.
- **`zip`**, compression, which leaks the plaintext's content through the token's length and turns a small token into a large plaintext. It is `malformed` at `["header", "zip"]`.
- **`crit`**, as for signed tokens: `unsupported_crit`.

## Signed, then encrypted

A token that must be both private and authentic is signed, then encrypted (RFC 7519 §5.2). `encryptJwt` does both, taking `sign`'s input as `sign` and writing `cty: "JWT"`:

```ts
import { createDecrypter, createJweKeySet, createNestedVerifier, createVerifier, encryptJwt } from "@codenhub/jwt";

const token = await encryptJwt({
  sign: { payload: { iss: "https://issuer.example", sub: "user-1", aud: "client-1", exp }, key: signingKey },
  key: clientEncryptionKey,
  enc: "A256GCM",
});

const verify = createNestedVerifier({
  decrypt: createDecrypter({ keys: createJweKeySet([clientDecryptionKey]) }),
  verify: createVerifier({ keys: issuerKeys, issuer: "https://issuer.example", audience: "client-1" }),
});
const result = await verify(token);
if (result.ok) {
  result.value.payload; // the verified claims
  result.value.encryption.header; // the outer JWE header
}
```

The nested verifier decrypts, requires a `cty` of `JWT` (in any casing, with or without `application/`) or none, and hands the plaintext to your verifier, which checks the inner token exactly as it would a bare one. A token that decrypts but does not verify fails with the verifier's issues, each with its path under `["plaintext", ...]`, so an inner `["header", "kid"]` is `["plaintext", "header", "kid"]` and an issue without a path gets `["plaintext"]`; the outer token's issues keep their own paths. A different `cty` is `wrong_type` at `["header", "cty"]`.

## A recipient's encryption keys

To encrypt to someone, such as the client an OpenID Provider encrypts ID tokens for, you need their public key, usually from their JWKS. `importEncryptionKeySet` and `createRemoteEncryptionKeySet` read one, and give an `EncryptionKeySet` whose `select` takes the algorithm you will use and, when you know it, the `kid`:

```ts
import { createRemoteEncryptionKeySet, encrypt } from "@codenhub/jwt";

const clientKeys = createRemoteEncryptionKeySet({ url: client.jwks_uri, algorithms: ["RSA-OAEP-256"] });
const selected = await clientKeys.select({ alg: "RSA-OAEP-256" });
if (selected.ok) {
  const token = await encrypt({ plaintext: idToken, key: selected.value, enc: "A256GCM" });
}
```

Only JWKs that say they encrypt are imported: `use: "enc"`, or, without `use`, a `key_ops` holding `encrypt`, `wrapKey`, `deriveKey` or `deriveBits`. A JWK with neither is skipped, so a JWKS that also lists signing keys never lends one to encryption. A JWK without `alg` is bound to each listed algorithm its key type fits, and `algorithms` defaults to every asymmetric key management algorithm. `issuer` is a signing option and throws here, and `importKeySet` and `createRemoteKeySet` never import an encryption key. Fetching, caching and cooldown work as [Key sets](docs/key-sets.md#a-remote-key-set) describes.

To rotate your own encryption keys as a recipient, publishing the current one and decrypting with older ones until senders no longer use them, see [Key rotation](docs/rotation.md#encryption-keys).

## Algorithms

| `alg`            | Key management                                        | Key                                      |
| ---------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `dir`            | the secret is the content key                         | secret as long as its `enc` key          |
| `A128KW`         | AES key wrap                                          | 16-byte secret                           |
| `A256KW`         | AES key wrap                                          | 32-byte secret                           |
| `A128GCMKW`      | AES-GCM key wrap, `iv` and `tag` in the header        | 16-byte secret                           |
| `A256GCMKW`      | AES-GCM key wrap, `iv` and `tag` in the header        | 32-byte secret                           |
| `ECDH-ES`        | ephemeral ECDH, Concat KDF derives the content key    | `EC` on P-256, P-384 or P-521, or X25519 |
| `ECDH-ES+A128KW` | ephemeral ECDH, Concat KDF derives a 16-byte wrap key | `EC` on P-256, P-384 or P-521, or X25519 |
| `ECDH-ES+A256KW` | ephemeral ECDH, Concat KDF derives a 32-byte wrap key | `EC` on P-256, P-384 or P-521, or X25519 |
| `RSA-OAEP`       | RSAES-OAEP with SHA-1                                 | `RSA`, 2048 to 8192 bit                  |
| `RSA-OAEP-256`   | RSAES-OAEP with SHA-256                               | `RSA`, 2048 to 8192 bit                  |
| `RSA-OAEP-384`   | RSAES-OAEP with SHA-384                               | `RSA`, 2048 to 8192 bit                  |
| `RSA-OAEP-512`   | RSAES-OAEP with SHA-512                               | `RSA`, 2048 to 8192 bit                  |

| `enc`           | Content encryption                     | Content key |
| --------------- | -------------------------------------- | ----------- |
| `A128GCM`       | AES-GCM                                | 16 bytes    |
| `A256GCM`       | AES-GCM                                | 32 bytes    |
| `A128CBC-HS256` | AES-CBC with HMAC SHA-256, 16-byte tag | 32 bytes    |
| `A256CBC-HS512` | AES-CBC with HMAC SHA-512, 32-byte tag | 64 bytes    |

`RSA-OAEP` is here because providers still publish it; SHA-1's weaknesses do not reach OAEP, but prefer `RSA-OAEP-256` where both sides support it. The 192-bit variants, `A192KW`, `A192GCMKW`, `ECDH-ES+A192KW`, `A192GCM` and `A192CBC-HS384`, are not supported, because Chromium's Web Crypto has no 192-bit AES; a token using one fails with `unsupported_alg` or `unsupported_enc`.

X25519 needs Web Crypto's X25519 support: Node.js 26, Cloudflare Workers, Chrome and Firefox have it, and Playwright's WebKit on Windows does not. The other algorithms work wherever Web Crypto does. The lists may grow in a minor release, so give a `switch` over an `alg` or `enc` a default branch.

<!-- Source: docs/jws.md -->

# JWS

A JWT is one use of a JSON Web Signature (JWS, RFC 7515): a JSON payload, compact form, read as claims. `signJws`, `signGeneralJws` and `createJwsVerifier` handle the rest of RFC 7515: any payload, bytes or text, in the compact serialization or the JSON one, with payloads left unencoded (RFC 7797) or kept out of the JWS altogether (detached, RFC 7515 Appendix F).

Use them when the thing you sign is not a set of claims: a webhook body, a document, a request digest, a payload another protocol defines. A JWS has no claims, so the verifier checks no `exp`, `aud` or `iss`, and a key set's issuer binding does not apply: a key bound to one issuer verifies a JWS like any other key in its set. A multi-tenant service picks the tenant's own key set, and the verifier made from it, before it verifies. For tokens, use [`sign`](docs/signing.md) and [`createVerifier`](docs/verifying.md), which stay compact-only.

```ts
import { createJwsVerifier, createKeySet, generateKeyPair, signJws } from "@codenhub/jwt";

const { privateKey, publicKey } = await generateKeyPair({ alg: "EdDSA", kid: "2026-11" });

const jws = await signJws({ payload: new Uint8Array([1, 2, 3]), key: privateKey });
// "eyJhbGciOiJFZERTQSIsImtpZCI6IjIwMjYtMTEifQ.AQID.…"

const verify = createJwsVerifier({ keys: createKeySet([publicKey]) });
const result = await verify(jws);
if (result.ok) {
  result.value.payload; // Uint8Array [1, 2, 3]
}
```

The algorithm is still the key's: `alg` is written from the key when signing and must equal the selected key's when verifying, so the verifier has no `algorithms` option.

## Signing

`signJws` writes one signature. Its `payload` is a `Uint8Array`, from any realm, or a string, signed as its UTF-8 bytes; a string with a lone surrogate throws, since it has no UTF-8 form.

| Member              | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `payload`           | The bytes or text to sign.                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `key`               | A private or secret key. Its `alg` and `kid` go into the protected header, as `sign` writes them.                                                                                                                                                |
| `header`            | Extra protected header members, checked as `sign` checks its `header`. It may hold `crit`; it may not hold `b64`, `jwk`, `jku`, `x5u` or `x5c`.                                                                                                  |
| `unprotectedHeader` | Members the signature does not cover, JSON serialization only. It may not hold `alg`, `crit`, `b64`, `jwk`, `jku`, `x5u` or `x5c`, nor share a member with the protected header. A `kid` here keeps the key's `kid` out of the protected header. |
| `b64`               | `false` to sign the payload unencoded (RFC 7797). Defaults to `true`.                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `detached`          | `true` to leave the payload out of the JWS. Defaults to `false`.                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `serialization`     | `"compact"`, the default, or `"flattened"` for the flattened JSON serialization.                                                                                                                                                                 |

`signGeneralJws` writes the general JSON serialization: one payload signed by 1 to 8 signers, each `{ key, header?, unprotectedHeader? }`, in the order given.

```ts
const jws = await signGeneralJws({
  payload: '{"amount":"10.00"}',
  signers: [{ key: ecPrivateKey }, { key: rsaPrivateKey, unprotectedHeader: { kid: "rsa-2026" } }],
});
// '{"payload":"eyJhbW91bnQiOiIxMC4wMCJ9","signatures":[{"protected":"…","signature":"…"},{…}]}'
```

Both return the JWS as a string, JSON text for the JSON serializations, and reject with a `TypeError` for a mistake in their input, as `sign` does.

Do not sign a JWS and a JWT with the same key. Neither `signJws` nor `sign` writes a `typ`, and a verifier without `type` requires none, so a compact JWS over JSON that holds `sub` and `exp` verifies as a JWT under `createVerifier` with that key, and a webhook body could be presented as an access token. Use a separate key for JWS, or give the JWS a distinct type with `header: { typ: "…" }` and set [`type`](docs/verifying.md#token-type) on every token verifier that trusts the key (RFC 8725 §3.11 and §3.12).

## Unencoded and detached payloads

With `b64: false`, the payload is signed as its bytes instead of its base64url text, and the protected header says so with `"b64":false` and `"crit":["b64"]`, which `signJws` writes for you. RFC 7797 lists it in `crit` so a verifier that does not understand `b64` refuses the JWS instead of checking the wrong bytes.

An unencoded payload has to survive the serialization it is written in. In the compact form it must be printable ASCII without `.`, which would end the segment; in the JSON form it must be UTF-8 text. Anything else throws: detach it instead.

A detached payload is signed but not written: the compact form has an empty middle segment, `<header>..<signature>`, and the JSON forms have no `payload` member. The receiver gets the payload some other way, such as an HTTP body, and gives it to the verifier:

```ts
const jws = await signJws({ payload: body, key: privateKey, b64: false, detached: true });
// send `jws` in a header and `body` as the body; on the other side:
const result = await verify(jws, { payload: body });
```

A detached compact JWS verified without its payload fails with `bad_signature`, not `missing_payload`: in the compact form an empty middle segment is the empty payload, which is a payload a JWS may sign, so the verifier checks the signature over it. Only a JSON JWS without a `payload` member is `missing_payload`.

## Verifying

`createJwsVerifier({ keys, crit?, maxLength?, onKeySetError? })` reads any of the three serializations: a string that starts with `{`, after JSON whitespace, is JSON, and anything else is compact. It takes the JSON serializations as their raw text, not as a parsed object: only the text shows a member repeated, which `JSON.parse` would resolve silently to its last value, and a JWS that repeats a member is refused. `keys` is a key set, as for `createVerifier`; a function that routes by issuer is not accepted, since a JWS has no `iss`, and the key set's issuer bindings are not applied. To verify each sender's JWS with its own keys, choose the verifier from the request, such as the webhook's URL or the sender's credentials, and keep one verifier per key set: there is no reader for a JSON or unencoded JWS's header before verification, and a header the signature has not covered would be the sender's word for whose key to trust. `maxLength`, 8192 characters by default and at most 65536, bounds the JWS, not a detached payload.

A JWS verifier also accepts a JWT signed by a key in its set, so the warning in [Signing](#signing) applies here too: a verifier that trusts a token signing key accepts that key's JWTs as JWS payloads, and a token verifier without `type` accepts that key's JWS over JSON claims as tokens.

Each JWS goes through, in order:

1. The length cap, before any decoding, and the input's type and well-formedness.
2. Strict parsing of its structure and of every signature's headers. JSON that repeats a member name, at any depth, or nests deeper than 32 levels is refused, and a general JWS may hold at most 8 signatures. Members of the JWS object that RFC 7515 does not define are ignored.
3. The header rules below, for every signature. Any issue here fails the whole JWS, even when another signature is good.
4. The payload: one given to the verifier is used only when the JWS carries none, and giving one for a JWS that carries its own is `malformed` at `["payload"]`.
5. Each signature in turn, until one verifies: its `alg`, its `crit` names, key selection from both of its headers, the key's algorithm, and the signature.
6. The payload's bytes, decoded only now.

The result is the frozen `{ payload, header, unprotectedHeader?, key, signatureIndex }`. `payload` is a `Uint8Array` of its own; decode text with `new TextDecoder("utf-8", { fatal: true })`. `header` is the protected header of the signature that verified, and `unprotectedHeader` its unprotected header, when it has one. Nothing in the unprotected header is signed: anyone who handles the JWS can change it, so never base a decision on it beyond choosing a key.

A general JWS verifies by its first signature that checks out, and `signatureIndex` says which. When none does, the failure lists every signature's issue, each under `["signatures", index]`:

```ts
{ ok: false, error: { issues: [
  { code: "unknown_kid", path: ["signatures", 0, "header", "kid"] },
  { code: "bad_signature", path: ["signatures", 1] },
] } }
```

### Header rules

- `alg`, `crit` and `b64` must be in the protected header, since they decide how the signature is checked.
- The protected and unprotected headers must not share a member (RFC 7515 §7.2.1).
- `crit` (RFC 7515 §4.1.11) is a non-empty list of distinct names, each present in the protected header, none of them a parameter RFC 7515 or RFC 7518 defines. A JWS whose `crit` names anything other than `b64` and the names in the verifier's `crit` option fails with `unsupported_crit`. List a name in `crit` only when your code processes that header member.
- `b64` is a boolean, listed in `crit`, and every signature of a general JWS agrees on it.
- `kid`, `typ` and `cty` are text.

A JWT verifies as a JWS too, its payload returned as bytes and none of its claims checked. The reverse is not true: `createVerifier` refuses `b64` and any `crit`, since RFC 7797 keeps unencoded payloads out of JWTs.

## Limits

| Limit                       | Value                                                  |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| JWS length                  | `maxLength`, 8192 characters by default, 65536 at most |
| Signatures in a general JWS | 8, signing and verifying                               |
| JSON nesting                | 32 levels                                              |

[Issues](docs/errors.md#jws) lists the codes a JWS verifier returns.

<!-- Source: docs/errors.md -->

# Issues

Everything that reads input you do not control, a token, a JWK, a JWKS or a key-set response, returns a result instead of throwing. For a verifier, a forged token is an ordinary Tuesday, not an exception. This page describes what a failed result holds and lists every code.

## The failed result

```ts
// What a verifier returned for an expired token with the wrong audience
const result = {
  ok: false,
  error: {
    issues: [
      { code: "expired", path: ["payload", "exp"] },
      { code: "wrong_audience", path: ["payload", "aud"] },
    ],
  },
};
```

`error.issues` is never empty, and its type says so, so `result.error.issues[0]` is an issue and not `undefined`. Issues are listed in the order the checks ran. Structural, key-selection and signature failures stop at the first one, so a result for them holds one issue; claim checks report every failing claim; a key import reports the first problem it finds.

The whole result is deeply frozen.

## The issue

| Field    | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `code`   | The stable category of the failure. Branch on it.                                                                                                                                                          |
| `path`   | Where the failure is, when it concerns one place: `["header", "kid"]`, `["payload", "exp"]`, a JWK member such as `["n"]`, or a segment such as `["signature"]`. Omitted when it concerns the whole input. |
| `params` | Facts from your own configuration or this package's limits, such as `{ maximum: 8192 }` or `{ claim: "sub" }`. Omitted when there are none.                                                                |

An issue this package creates never holds a value taken from the input: no token segment, claim value, header value, or key material, and no message from Web Crypto, a schema or a server, since any of those can quote the input. It names which check failed and never what the token said, so a failure can be logged, returned to a client or sent to an error tracker without leaking a token. `path` names claims and header members, which are names this package or your configuration chose, never values. `params.status` of `key_fetch_failed` is the HTTP status code the JWKS server answered with, a number and never content.

Two kinds of issue come from your code, and hold only what it puts in them: a `schema_failed` path is your schema's path, so a schema over a record can name a payload's own property names there, and a custom key set's failure issues are returned as it gave them. Keep both free of input values if you log them.

Codes and `params.reason` values may gain members in a minor release, when a new check or failure needs its own name; existing ones keep their meaning. Treat an unknown code as a failure like any other, and give a `switch` over codes a `default` branch rather than relying on TypeScript's exhaustiveness check.

There are no messages: a code is the whole answer. Map codes to text yourself if a person needs to read them, and prefer not to tell a client more than "invalid token" when the client may be an attacker.

## Codes

### Token structure

| Code               | Path                                | Params                            | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ------------------ | ----------------------------------- | --------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `malformed`        | none, a segment, or a header member |                                   | Not a string, not three segments, a segment that is empty or not strict base64url, or JSON that is invalid or not an object. Also a non-text `kid`, `typ` or `cty`, and any `b64` header. |
| `too_large`        | none                                | `{ limit: "length", maximum }`    | The token is longer than `maxLength`.                                                                                                                                                     |
| `too_large`        | `["header"]` or `["payload"]`       | `{ limit: "depth", maximum: 32 }` | The JSON nests deeper than 32 levels.                                                                                                                                                     |
| `duplicate_key`    | `["header"]` or `["payload"]`       |                                   | A JSON object repeats a member name, at any depth.                                                                                                                                        |
| `unsupported_alg`  | `["header", "alg"]`                 |                                   | `alg` is missing or not one of the supported algorithms, compared exactly. `none` in any casing is here.                                                                                  |
| `unsupported_crit` | `["header", "crit"]`                |                                   | The header has a `crit` member. A JWT understands no header extension.                                                                                                                    |

### Key selection and signature

| Code               | Path                | Params                                  | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| ------------------ | ------------------- | --------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `unknown_kid`      | `["header", "kid"]` |                                         | No key in the set has the header's `kid`. A remote set refetches first, outside its cooldown.                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
